answer: As you know, we do have still a buyback program in place, and it's something the Board will -- does consider each quarter. So it's something that certainly is on the agenda to discuss.

question: Got it. And I think at the time, you've sort of put out something publicly on that in the fourth quarter of last year. I believe that there was some mix between what would be paid in cash and what would be paid in stock. I guess, a, do you -- I think at that point in time, it was about 20% cash. Should investors expect something similar to that if a REIT conversion occurs? And how much control do you have over the cash versus stock component?
answer: Well, it used to be -- you had to go to the IRS and get a private letter ruling to get the 80-20 permission. And I think the general theory was enough cash to really cover the tax portion of the dividend. But now the SEC -- the IRS has come out and basically you sort of codified that, that you could do the 80-20 if you choose, but it's obviously up to the company in many ways, but also it's the conversions up to the shareholders in terms of approval. But in -- most recently, and I think it's really kind of a COVID-driven thing. The IRS has been allowing a 90-10 split, so 10% in cash. I'm not sure where the Board is going to come out on that. But the 80-20 is certainly the one that is permitted.

question: Got it. No, that makes sense. And one more from me. I know that you were pretty excited when you added Superica and the food hall operator at Ashford Lane. I'm curious, has that translated yet to increased leasing activity and interest at Ashford Lane.
answer:
So I'll give you a little bit of background on the food hall as far as where they are just as an opportunity since you bring it up. This whole supply chain thing is this like it's definitely hit the real estate side as well because the food hall is basically accessing a lot of their inventory FF&E from China. And I don't have to tell you what that means. So they're looking at more end of the year opening. And when we signed this up, we thought it was going to be summer of this year, so a couple of months ago. 
And so -- but they're making very good progress. They're about 80% built out -- but even on the build-out side, they're waiting for materials and so forth. But as far as leasing -- as you can see in our earnings we have an incredible amount of leasing activity there. But interesting to me, it really hasn't been driven by the food hall excitement. It's really the location that we have on Ashford Lane is so important for that whole area, that tenants, if they are looking for expanding in the burbs outside of Atlanta. 
This is where -- this is one of the hot areas. And so as you can think about it, the more core of Atlanta, a lot of those tenants are leaving for the burbs. And so we're just in a good spot. So it doesn't really have to do with the hall as much. Thank you very much for attending our earnings call and look forward to talking to you through the rest of the year. Thank you.

question: Could you give a little more color on your comment about the passenger tire demand in China, and I guess to some extent, is this replacement demand softness you're seeing and versus OE and then maybe some color both in China and North America, sort of your outlook on OE potential?
answer: So with regard to China, the comment was specifically related to the replacement market from our perspective and what we're seeing is that customers in China, and we believe this is an industry not just a Cooper phenomenon, is that as they're watching raw material costs continue to decline and they're anticipating what might be the effects from the potential tariff in the U.S. on tires, PCR tires coming from China and potentially resulting in some of those tires staying in China for sale that they're thinking that, that could have implications on the pricing for tires, so they're reluctant to build inventories of tires right now and until they have a better feel for how that's going to work itself through.

question: Okay. And I think you talked about maybe some higher promotional spend on SG&A in the second half of the year. Are your channels still the same? I think it was maybe last year's investor meeting you talked about sort of Professional Bull Riders Association and some of your marketing partners. Is there anything that you're doing differently as far as promoting or sort of brand building this year?
answer: Not a lot. Those have been pretty effective for us. When you think about the ESPN Halftime Show in the fall here on NCAA football and those type of things that we're involved with. The PBR, which is really kind of ongoing for the year. The Arsenal investment that we renewed this year has been very popular for us. So we -- the Canadian Hockey League, I mean, to build our brand, we've done a really good job building our brand in Canada and making some -- getting some traction there. So we're going to continue with those until we see something ship there, Bret, but those have been fairly successful for us.

question: This is Dan Drawbaugh on for Chris. If I could just go really quickly to the international capital deployment, can you talk in any way about the timing that we should think of between Latin America and China? I mean, you guys talked a lot about Latin America just on this call, not quite so much about China. So should we start looking at Latin America as the sooner of the two or is there anything else even sail along those lines?
answer: I think Latin America, we -- it actually was just a timing of when we're going to highlight it during the call to make sure that we're providing additional color on what we think is a very exciting market now. It did happen to correspond to some very good things going on in that market, but it wasn't intended to signal anything with regard to a change or anything specific around the timing of our capital expenditures. As Ginger noted, we got some very specific priorities with regard to capital allocation. Clearly, we continue to talk about some of the things that we're planning to do in China. And again, we hope to be able to talk maybe with more specifics before the end of the year, but there wasn't anything that we were trying to signal with the emphasis on the good things that are going on in Latin America earlier in the call.

question: Can you explain a little bit more about North America. Within North America the -- I guess, the pricing being flat while raw materials are down? And how that -- how that activity went typically -- moved in sync with each other? If you can just explore that a little bit, that would be helpful.
answer: I will. I'll start and then maybe Tom might want to add some commentary as well. I think one of the issues is the tariff. And so the tariff was implemented in November of '14 on all passenger car tires manufactured in China imported to the U.S. Those tires -- interestingly, imports are about the same for the first 6 months of '15. So tires that were coming from -- tires from China are lower, imports from China are lower, but they been replaced almost to the same extent by imports from other parts of the world. So there are still the same number of imports coming into the U.S. They're just coming in probably at a slightly higher price. Because of very lowest price, Chinese tires may not be coming and that maybe firming pricing in the industry. The tide has moved up on all of the tires in the industry. I think the -- so the tariff is clearly having some impact. I think the second factor is that demand has been very good in the U.S. this year. So you saw that 4% -- 4.9% year-to-date growth in tire demand. That's much higher than we've seen in recent years. So it could be in an environment where everyone is selling more units than they expected, but no one feels they need to compete on price. So that may be helping with the price discipline. I'll see if Tom's got an input because you were at the company during the last round of tariffs. Those are the 2 big things, and lot of the demand can be driven by the -- with gasoline prices as low as that is right now, miles-driven, which is a great leading indicator of tire purchases on the consumer end has been very strong. So I think that's one of the precursors leading to the demand that Ginger noted. Yes, it's worth noting that low gas prices help us in 2 ways. As Tom said, it does drive more miles driven, which drives replacement tires over time. And then secondly, it's a significant raw material input for us. So the combination of that pricing discipline, the lower raw materials has been -- has led to a very strong year in our U.S. business this year. Yes?

question: That's very helpful. Just on the beginning part. [indiscernible] start thinking about some of the self-help and actions that you've been taking. I mean, where do you feel like you are, if this is a ballgame, in the early innings, middle innings or late innings of some of those actions and having that margin expansion come to fruition?
answer: The things that we -- the improvements in mix and in cost, I mean, we're no further than the middle innings. And part of that's driven by the industry and part of that's driven by the fact that we are probably moving faster in some of those higher-margin products than even the industry is.

question: Great. That's very helpful. On the positive side, the international markets did very well. I'm wondering if you could just give us a little more detail. I know you said Europe and Asia were both contributors, but a little more detail on, was 1 outside versus the other. And then was it OEM versus replacement business and just what you're seeing in those marketplaces?
answer: Yes. Just to clarify a couple of the comments that I made in, it was in both, but so if we talk about Asia and Europe. Specifically, we talked about an 80% increase in domestic volumes in Asia in the first quarter year-over-year. That was -- it was both OEM replacement, but OE was clearly the stronger contributor to that growth. In Europe, we had double-digit increases close to 20% in that market, and a lot of that driven by a stronger U.K. market, which is important to our business both from a volume and a profit perspective, along with an overall continuation of refreshing of the product portfolio there and having more competitive products that are helping us in all of our markets in Europe.

question: And then -- you think about -- I mean, the industry saw some very, very strong margins over the past couple of years. How do you think about that relative to where you're at today and your ability to return to those levels? Is that something that you think Cooper and/or the industry can achieve again once things settle out? Or do you think that there's some impediments there?
answer: I think with regard to Cooper specifically, we do believe that we have structurally improved our margins over the last several years with some of the improvements that we've made to our business. There's still some opportunities to continue down the mix path as we've talked about around the cost path we've talked about including the way that we utilize our global manufacturing footprint. On the other side, from a macro perspective, with regard to the industry and where we're at in that price-raw material relationship, we don't see anything that is fundamentally different than the backdrop that we've been operating with for the last couple of years. You do go through these periods when there's volatility around raw material prices up, down, up and down where it takes a bit of time for pricing to realign itself to where raw materials settle in. And so there will be a bit of disruption. We've historically -- Brett, you've been watching us for a long time. And we talk about margin guidance over a cycle because we know that you go through these types of changes. But we don't see anything that suggests that the macro environment is different than what it was 18 months ago and that we won't see the industry continue to do what they were doing at that point in time on price-raw material specifically.

question: No, no, that's exactly what I understood it to be. My question is that's prohibited you or limited you from being more competitive in the marketplace. And so if pricing firms up in the industry in the first half of 2018, how long does that take for it to roll through Cooper Tire's pricing? Are there annual contracts that are going to prohibit that? Are you potentially going to set up a price structure in January 1 that even if pricing improves in the first quarter or second quarter, it prohibits you from adjusting your pricing?
answer: So the -- our invoice pricing will be market-based. And then the promotional and incentive programs that we put into the market will also be market-faced. But we'll essentially be starting from 0 at the beginning of 2018. So your -- we'll be in a position where we're resetting and can ensure that we are appropriately positioned to win.

question: Got you. And then one last question for me. If at all possible, can you talk about the cadence volume throughout the quarter, July, August, September? September seems like it stood out positively. Your price increases, October 1 announcement, was the 1st week of September. Wondering if there might have been a little bit of prebuy in September or not or really if you feel like the improvements versus July and August was more based on normalized run rate in terms of sell-out, sell-in?
answer: Sure, Anthony. The -- yes, I would sequentially -- clearly September we exited with a very strong month. Now I will say that I -- as we look at it and the way that we implemented that price reduction and frankly the order book that we've continued to see in October, we're not looking at September as being strongly affected by pull ahead. It's always a little bit difficult to discern exactly what would have come and what may have come because of a price increase. But if I look at it with regard to the exit rate of that month and as we moved into September, we still feel good about the momentum of our order book moving into the fourth quarter.

question: Good. So we've talked a lot about China, and we'll talk more about China in the rest of the Q&A. But shifting to the topic of Chinese New Year, I think expectations were for TV sales growth to be about 10%, 20% year-over-year during the holidays and interested -- I'm interested in your views on how that went, how would call it 10%, call it 20%? Were expectations met quality [ph] speaking in the supply chain?
answer: Yes. So far, the data is not complete. And as you all know, the Lunar New Year moves around a little bit, so it straddles the tailwind of January moving into February. But if you look on a 3-week window around that on a year-on-year basis, the preliminary data that we've seen is about a 15% increase. So we were pleased with that.

question: And so just to follow up on one point you made, especially on the density and kind of the inherently heavier nature of sapphire. I know it's something you can't change even if you put a lot of money on that. Should we infer from that, that most likely then, how you guys think the market plays out is that maybe that kind of material is appropriate for certain things like say, a watch, where that incremental cost is not a big deal versus some 4-inch -- and small, right, versus 4-inch smartphone or higher?
answer: Right, right. That's the way we think about it. And we think, actually, that this could be more of a marketing ploy than actual performance enhancement. I got a jewel on my cell phone, right? It's sapphire, right? But performance-wise, we've been through this. We actually make crystals ourselves, and we make crystal -- we make polysilicon crystal through a joint venture with Dow. Hemlock, right? So we know a fair amount about crystal growth and what it takes to do it successfully. So we think this will perhaps be commercialized but be limited.

question: And just on the Gorilla application, in terms of what might be better as we look into 2014 and '15, would it be the touch notebooks, would it be tablets? Or how would you kind of rank order relative to a year ago, where you see more promise in Gorilla Glass applications?
answer: We're expecting touch-on notebooks to grow this year. It's obviously a small number, but I think the growth -- touch-on notebooks would be 50% and we're gaining share in touch-on notebooks this year. So that's important for us. Tablets continue to be an excellent market and, obviously, tablets are a whole lot bigger than smartphones. So we feel good about both of those.

question: Okay. And then the second question was on the competitive environment in Gorilla Glass. It looks like from the volumes you're expecting that you're certainly looking to gain some share there. But you also talked about having some price declines as you're locking up some of these contracts. So can you just give us a sense a little bit of how the competitive environment looks like right now and what type of price declines should we be thinking about for this year for Gorilla Glass? Is it something on the order of 20% or not quite that high?
answer:
Well, I'll start at the end and then work my way up. So we would expect that Gorilla price declines to moderate very significantly as we go forward into Q2. Specifically on price, we had much larger-than-normal price declines in Q1 in Gorilla due to us ramping up full year contracts to maintain our market position. And what led to that really is just competitors being more aggressive on price than they have been. They've always been pretty aggressive, but they found a new level of aggression for this round. Now what's important to note is that our significant price premium versus the competition is continuing, or, actually, it's even increasing, but they just made a big move. So even though our premiums' in place, the baseline that it moves from moved downward. We would expect that type of premium for the performance segments, any time you have a product that you care about its performance, to continue because we're going to launch a new Gorilla that's even better than our current Gorilla this year, so we feel good about that. 
I think the next area of opportunity and challenge is the ultra-low performance segments that we're seeing now emerge in China. Another example is low but not ultra-low with touch-on notebook. And for that, what we're looking to do is create a real soda lime glass spider that can be really competitive with those offerings for the lower-performance segments. More on that as the year goes on. We got some innovation and market work ahead of us to make that happen as well.

question: Great. Okay, I've got a question from the web that -- actually, it's from Alvin Kwock, who's one our analysts in Asia, sitting right there. I'm going to ask it for you anyway, Alvin. So he's asking -- he's saying China has some localization policies going for TV panels which have started to get some critical mass, and there are talks about tariffs for glass now. Are you prepared for that? How do you think that, that plays out? Any local competitors that you're watching in China?
answer: So we are obviously prepared for the potential of tariffs and we have glass manufacturing in China. The Beijing factory is expandable, if necessary, so we clearly are prepared for that, recognizing right now there's a huge economic advantage to ship off existing capacity with variable costs in other countries, but we are prepared for that. In terms of local competition, obviously, there is encouragement of that by the government. We have not felt them, particularly on any large size. We think most of their efforts have been on smaller size Gen 5 and below, probably a little coming now on Gen 6. But we really have not felt that and continue to be well received by our customers in China with our large-scale glass.

question: I guess number one is pertaining to Gorilla Glass. I think you stated that volume growth should be in line with IT handheld, and that price declines would be more moderate than 2014 due to Gorilla Glass 4. I would love your view on what Corning's outlook is for IT handheld in 2015. And then the pricing decline commentary, 2014 was relatively aggressive. Could you help us kind of narrow the range a little bit?
answer: I'm not going to give specific numbers on price, but the reduction for the full year 2015 should be quite a bit lower than what it was in 2014. In terms of market growth, I think we have handheld square feet growing 15%. We're thinking media tablets could grow in the upper single digits, and then, of course, we will have some growth from touch on notebook. And just a reminder, we hope that all flows to us, but we have to always manage the supply chain and see how much inventory there is, but we do think that those are the kind of growth rates we'll see at retail.

question: Okay. And then, I guess, my last question before I maybe open up to the floor is Gorilla Glass, you mentioned in your presentation, has really been trending well. I think you mentioned at one point that it's actually been turned out to be more profitable success compared to other Gorilla Glass releases. Can you maybe elaborate on that and why...
answer: Yes, I think you're referring or launch of Gorilla Glass 4. So right now the best surface cover for phones out there is Gorilla Glass 3, with the exception of Gorilla Glass 4, which is even better where, because of its better performance, we're able to charge a price premium. And the adoption of Gorilla Glass 4 has been a bit faster than we expected and faster than earlier adoptions of new generation. So we're very encouraged by the continued desire of manufacturers for thin, durable optically terrific surfaces.

question: And in that context my follow-up was going to be you floated the idea of potential full stability in pricing and actually increases in glass pricing, if you go to a thin -- to a point that it's so thin that it requires kind of premium manufacturing capability. Is that still a theoretical possibility?
answer: Oh, I hope so. Yes, I think it is. And in the fusion processes, much of the way we operate it is uniquely advantaged for thin. There are thicknesses in the market today that we've commercialized that our competitors can't make, right? And we're selling it. We're selling it to specifically the OLED business. And the value prop for smaller sizes, as many know, most of these displays are thinned after they're manufactured to get a very thin end product. Of course, we can make it with native glass, right? It saves the thinning process, which is expensive, uses hydrofluoric acids, nasty staff. And you don't waste all that material, right? And that's the driver to thinner and thinner glass. So if it goes that direction and it has been going in that direction, we think we're uniquely advantaged in that space.

question: I also had a couple of questions on the Optical business. And to start, maybe how come we shouldn't expect better than low-teens growth for the year, given the out-performance in Q1? And I was hoping you could help us understand the OpEx component of your fiber expansion plans, and to what extent the profitability of the Optical business might be impacted as you invest in more capacity this year?
answer: This is Tony, why don't I take those 2 questions? Some of that growth that we experienced in the first quarter, of course, was not repeating the software implementation issue that we had a year ago. But even in spite of that, we were up about 15%, and our guidance for the full year is low teens. So from our standpoint, that's very good significant growth. It's certainly better than what the industry averages. Capital spending in the optical arena, and it's well on track to get us to the $5 billion of sales, which is our objective by 2020. So I think, overall, we feel very good about the optical growth. In terms of the capacity expansions, I mean, the thing to remember, the power of our framework is, is that we already have a lot of capacity in Optical Communications. And so why we are adding some capacity there, it does have a negative impact in this on the short term, it's not significant, and you can -- you will see it a little bit with slightly lower gross margins as we ramp up some of the production, but it's well within our guidance of 42% to 43% for the year, so I don't think it's going to have a big significant impact.

question: And just the question on auto for -- Gorilla Glass for auto?
answer: Yes, we're seeing really nice momentum. Now that being said, this is an industry that moves at a very deliberate pace. So we tend not to try to get overly excited because you win today for revenue, that's in the farther future. But we're feeling really good and it's interesting. In any innovation that is pretty disruptive like this one is, then what you tend to try to do is you'll get positive surprises and negative surprises. And when you get the positive surprises, you start to double down on them. I'd say we're getting some really nice positive surprises right now, in automotive interiors. People's vision for what they want to do in the interior of vehicles is quite stirring, and it's driving them very much into the arms of our material setting, our co-innovation approach. So we're actually been investing an awful lot of time and attention into that, and we're getting really, really nice pull. So I think that's what you're sort of sensing is the exteriors is going about how we've been anticipate with the normal deliberate pacing, and we're getting really nice positive surprises that we're doubling down on in interiors. And what's interesting is the type of innovations that they want, a very high revenue generation want because of the value-add they want from us around optics, around shape. So that revenue opportunities looking very attractive.

question: Given the panel oversupply, there's some concern out there that some of your customers could convert or perhaps shut down older plants. How should investors think about the impact of this panel supply on Corning?
answer: I think, at the end of day, what really drives our demand is the end market and how many people -- how many TVs are sold and what size those TVs are. And so from -- as we look at this year, we thought we would be up mid-single digits driven both in terms of the -- where the TV unit growth is, but, most importantly, the screen size growth. And as we look forward, we -- that screen size growth has continued for a number of years and we expect that to continue going forward. So I think the way people should think about, our demand is really driven by the TV market. Haley, we still have time -- we've got time for one more question.

question: Got it. Got it. Yes. Probably the biggest discussion maybe at this conference or maybe many conferences in the first half of 2019 are going to be all solely on 5G impacts. Shifting gears on Gorilla Glass 6, you guys discussed on your last earnings call. I was hoping we could maybe just reiterate kind of what you were -- what discussed -- what was discussed in the earnings call and then maybe just a little bit more about this recent development and rollout.
answer: Yes. So Gorilla Glass has been a great growth driver for us over its full lifetime, and certainly, within the last 3 years. What's going on is the design of phones is increasing the value of premium glasses. So Gorilla Glass 6 reaches a new level of durability versus Gorilla Glass 5 and resets the standard for the industry. That makes glass even more attractive for both the front and the back of phones. Using glass on the backs of phones is attractive, not only from the aesthetics of the design but also from performance capabilities. It helps wireless charging and it gives more design degrees of freedom for the RF portion of the phone, which will be particularly important as we move to 5G where the real estate for antennas is expected to be greater than for LTE or earlier standards. So those are the big drivers for us. We think that there is a lot more innovation that will be attractive both to designers and to end customers in terms of performance so that we have a lot of innovation left in this space to deliver over time.

question: Just wanted to ask about -- I think one of the concerns that investors have right now is probably around visibility into end markets back through the supply chain to what you're supplying. And in particular, I think the narrative on larger display size as well as in the Optical business makes sense. But I'm wondering if you can talk a little bit about things that you are doing or can do to further improve your visibility and are you able to see changes in demand trajectory first? My second -- my follow-up question is, at the Analyst Day last month, you gave a pretty upbeat assessment of the opportunities in both Valor Glass and automotive opportunities. Just wondering if there has been any additional data points you can contribute to those new products.
answer:
So I think on -- let's do the value chain first and then I'll try to tie in the other piece. So for us, it's a little like the walk-through that I just did on Optical. We've got 2 levels that we try to align. The first is the long-term technology substitution curves for our innovations. And as you remember from the Investor Day, the core of our growth story is a content story, which is what we expect over the coming 4 years is more and more of our innovations to be adopted into the products that people buy. And that is our primary growth driver as opposed to how much of everything everybody buys or what type of economy do we face.
We continue to get nothing, but positive signals on those items, whether it's in Optical or in the areas that you just named, automotive. So here we are in a time period when you see declining forecasts of overall automotive sales and production, but we are projecting growth in the teens because of more and more of our content. Similar things we would expect to happen in the Valor story. We once again tend to have confirmatory evidence that we're on the right side of that substitution curve. Optical, very much the same as you heard in my answer. And in Specialty Materials, our Mobile Consumer Electronics business, also much the same.
So that's the first level. We feel pretty good about that. The next then comes to how does the timing of that substitution curve play out and how does that interact with overall demand for our customers? Now that you can get a little more noise in, in the near term and we're certainly experiencing some of that. So then we have folks like Jeff Evenson who's here in the room as well as pretty significant analytical groups to try to start right at the end market and then work the way all the way back to the value chain and build models and the right analytic tools to keep track of it. We don't always get it exactly right, but we feel pretty good that we're able to track the core demand signals through the system.

question: So some of the 5G radio technologies become very sensitive.
answer: You're absolutely right. Yes.

question: Prior to this quarter, when the macro wasn't that concerning, you had talked about the Optical Communication business getting back to growth in the second half, and I understand that has changed quite significantly. But maybe just give us an update on where you're thinking, stand on that? And how much of this is just kind of -- even if your thinking has changed, how much of this is just the shelter-in-place restrictions, et cetera, just pushing out stuff temporarily versus companies really evaluating their CapEx plans?
answer:
I think you've got a combination. On one hand, telecom has been deemed essential, and the companies have really done amazing work to keep the networks operational and to be able to upgrade to provide service. And they've deployed so many field personnel to do that. But there's no question that anything that was optional to do was spread out, was pushed out in time. It's a very challenging time to do network installation. 
Then we'll also have whatever this economic impact plays out, and each company is different. They have different balance sheets. They have different mix of businesses. But I do believe, whether or not it happens in the second half or whether or not it happens after that, I feel like the -- it's overall a bull signal for high-capacity networks. And this is back to new trends don't usually get created, but trends that were in place get accelerated. So I think we're just going to have more and more substitution of optical and our content will continue to go up and up. I still think that's the main message out of this. When? I just don't know yet. I mean, as soon as I do and we can do it with confidence, we'll tell you guys.

question: No. Okay. Fair enough. How about laptops? Not Ceramic Shield but just glass bodies on laptops. We have a lot more connectivity, especially 5G, it looks like it makes sense to probably, at some point, deploy cellular modems more in laptops. Do you think that ushers in an era of kind of glass-bodied laptops pretty soon? Or is that sort of still way out in the future?
answer: I don't -- I mean,it's probably somewhere in between. And of course, it will start with the higher-end premium laptops. And as you know, that market is booming right now. But I think the idea that you would get -- that, that would be a good solution to a problem that's going to definitely continue to grow over the next few years, the connectivity in 5G, I mean, that is definitely a possible driver in this business.

question: Okay, okay. That's great. That's incremental. And maybe as a follow-up, and just to keep Ann involved. Would you eventually break Gorilla? Or would you -- should we assume that the interior center opportunity would be added to the auto segment of your revenue breakdown?
answer: So in terms of where the sales -- where you would see the sales is going to be in the Other segment.

question: I think that's a very clear answer to this already. Okay. Let's go back to some of the key trends. Last one after EV and the 5G, the next one I want to cover is for the different display technology because we moved from LCD to OLED. And going forward, there is already MiniLED, MicroLED and many, many new technologies in the pipeline. How do you think some of those future technologies will impact the glass demand in the production of those displays?
answer:
Terrific. So it's so fascinating to talk about new display technologies. I think the first thing to realize is that just how stately of precession new technology is in display. New tech takes a very long time. And the reason is it's almost always the incumbent tech keeps getting better at a very fast rate. So gosh, it had to be first time like 15 years ago when folks started to ask me about OLED TV. And what I said is like that's a great question. However, where we're going to place our bet is LCD TV will be a much better value for customers, and it will win that battle. And OLED TV will be -- it'll have a position, but it will be small.  
And that's exactly what's happened. It doesn't mean that the question doesn't come up like all the time still. It does. But you can really understand the technology node well and deeply, plan for it and attack it if you just really take the time. So that's an example. 
The thing we liked in OLEDs was for handheld, especially for polyimide displays, because you could make them conform, you could make them bend. Now that's something LCD doesn't do well. So we were really interested in that. And so we placed our bet on the technology to enable that, and all of those displays are built on our proprietary substrate material that, by the way, uses more glass than traditional LCD because you build it on our mother material. 
As we look forward, what we see is the most interesting technology is probably MicroLED. It's a beautiful technology. It's really cool. It's going to take a really long time, okay? A really long time. And -- but we've been investing in that space for, I don't know, God, it will almost be double-digit years. In a contained way, working with our key customers to see what can we do to solve the deep technical problems that are there. So we like it because once again, it's very different than LCD. In LCD, the economics are just so good. The pictures are just so good, right? And they've got so much runway that any new tech has to do something different. But the good news is it will be slow. Investors always ask, and I always feel like saying, like, there's nothing that's going to sneak up on anybody in display technology, right?

question: Well, last one, and then I'll step back. It appears currency is still benefiting supplier cost, can you talk about to what extent you're having to pass these savings on the terms of lower prices to retail?

question: Okay, that was good color. Then do you plan to use the Carousel website to sell any of your nonbedding products? And are there any products that you offer that could benefit from its customization platform?
answer: Well, I mean -- let me answer the second one first. There's products that we sell that could benefit from the customization, that's very true. Do we plan to use the Carousel website? question: So your gross margin performance has been pretty good for a couple of quarters now with year-over-year increase in gross margin. What are the specific reasons for that? And I am just trying to figure out if that's a trend that will continue in the second half of the fiscal year?
answer: Well, I mean, I'll answer them separately, Linda. For the second half of the year, as you well know, we don't give forecast, and we don't guide -- give guidance. So you have to judge us, you, sort of, got to look in the rearview mirror. And the reason for the increase is a slight change in product mix, but most importantly, it's really the ongoing efforts of the company to maintain cost control, which we've done now for many years, and we continue to do it. And that's one of the things that we pride ourselves on is running a very tight operating company.

question: That's very good. And the second question is that advertising cost ...

answer: No. Other than Carousel, nothing in this quarter. We had the forgiveness of the Paycheck Protection loan in the first quarter, but that obviously wasn't [indiscernible]. And then otherwise, it's -- other than the increased costs that we've talked about in the cost of sales, so there's nothing unusual.

question: And then last question for me. Are you actively looking for potential acquisitions at the moment?
answer: Yes, we are very clear in terms of what is a fit and not a fit. We've nothing to report on this call, but we are much clearer with every passing month and quarter. We're obviously working in that area, but we're not going to rush it. If we find the right thing, we can act quickly, provided again, it's the right fit to the strategy and, of course, with the right valuation of price, so we maximize return for shareholders.

question: And how much is the Canadian restructuring going to benefit the top line?
answer: It will be smaller than what we had from the initial restructuring that was started in the middle of 2013. I'm expecting a incremental gross margin improvement as a result, but it's not going to be a significant number.

answer: I would give you -- we don't guide down to below that level, but the majority of that is -- we said was a 3-year contract in the HDD space. Which is the extension of our existing HDD business.

answer: We actively look at the currency rates as well, Ian, as it does impact the business. As we look ahead, we do a couple of things. That will be published later on today as well.

question: Okay. And then any other growth drivers that we may not be aware of for 2018, Kieran?
answer: No, we would pick some of the big things in terms of the sensor platforms, the accelerators. And certainly, on the electronic components, we've got some good momentum going and adding new customers. And we continue to add new customers. I think your guidance range is probably a good measure of our growth.

answer: Let me make sure I understand your question. Are you asking where the gross margin is expected to be after the completion of the restructuring action?

question: Got it. And then Kieran, when we read the news about like shortages in automotive semiconductor, how should we relate that to CTS? Earlier, you mentioned that CTS exposure to European is less. Like any guidepost on how we should think about the supply chain shortages in automotive semiconductor, if it's improved or if it gets worse?
answer: So Hendi, 2 things. First thing is we don't have any supplies ourselves for our products. That's the first thing I'd like to point out. So it's our OEM. So if they're getting the electronics or the semiconductors for their electronic control units and infotainment systems and other things, that's the watch. So we've seen things from General Motors. We don't have any -- seen things from Ford. We don't have any big exposure with Ford. We've said so far in the first quarter, we would see that at this point in time, less than $0.5 million impact. So we haven't seen heavy impact. We've seen the number of units impacted from the industry reports go from about 600,000 units to about 850,000, and that's something we're tracking live. And you may see the next report before we do. But I haven't heard anything. We know there's a lot of pressure out there from the OEMs and back to the suppliers in Taiwan and other areas to ramp-up production, and I'm sure they're really focused on that at this point in time.

question: Sure. Two other quick ones for you. Do you anticipate seeing annual or quarterly guidance now that you're increasing investor communications?
answer: Well, we're taking one step at a time. I -- we don't have any immediate plans to give guidance, but it's something we'll be discussing between now and the end of the next quarter. So we're not going to -- we have not yet decided to do that.

question: Great. What percent of your simulation training is from contracts overseas?
answer: It's about -- in the systems business, it's roughly 50-50 between U.S. and the rest of the world.

answer: Let me just add to that. In credit to our founder for creating an international company, a lot of companies are trying to do more international. But if you have great mass of opportunities, a lot of them can get in the end zone.

question: Just wanted to start off first on the New York City opportunity. Seems like its scope is expanding. answer: Yes, the total contract, I believe, will be over $1 billion and I think will expand further. So it is increasing. Boston is a key opportunity. answer: We'll see some growth this year but next year we'll see even better and better growth.

answer: Yes, both of those contracts are relatively early days. What I mean is we're doing design kinds of activities. I'd like to thank my outstanding teammates for their focus on winning the trust of our customers. Thank you all for your partnership and for joining us today.

question: Brad, just maybe on the contract you called out, the High Capacity Backbone. I mean, it sounds like a great opportunity. And I'm just -- I think, Jon, was hitting on this about the mix. answer: Yes. So overall, we've been doing a lot of nonrecurring from major wins that we had last year: the MQ-25; the Joint Strike Fighter; the MH-60; and Boomslang, those were major wins for us. The High Capacity Backbone starting portion of the contract, the $38 million. The margins there are lower single digit, but when you move into the production phase of these programs, they're double-digit margins and will move us to the mid-teen area that we've talked about in this business. I'll also note that in that portfolio, GATR has very nice margins, DTECH has very nice margins, the Pixia software business that we picked up, has great margins. So I would expect that margins to continue to expand as we go.

question: Just a little bit back to Ann's question on the NAFTA truck market. The end-use customers are obviously seeing some challenges. I'm wondering if you've seen any industry order activity acceleration during October.
answer: No, we haven't, Andy. We'll be delayed from the truck guys, obviously. And you see -- and obviously, you'll talk to them, I assume, and see. But right now, if you look at build rates or whatever, we're not seeing anything accelerating in build rates.

question: Could you talk a little bit more about the high horsepower engines? When they're going to be coming on and what impact that's going to be like -- more like the fourth -- 15-story, but the overall market potential there over the next several years.
answer: So when let me kick it off and Mark can jump in. So this is a 85-liter engine that we've been developing for a number of years now and probably the largest single investment in the company's history. So it's a big deal for us. It will take us into segments of markets where we don't have an offering to date and where our competition enjoys a very good and lucrative market. So you'll see in Power Generation first of all. You'll see it in commercial marine, in locomotive, in oil and gas. So good segments for us to be in, both in terms of first fit [ph] demand but also in terms of the aftermarket and the opportunity in the aftermarket. In terms of the impact on 2015 financials. It's not going to be significant in terms of 2015 dollars. It'll be more significant by 2018, but we've never revealed that number publicly, so it will be inappropriate for me to share that just now. Word upstairs is there's like some early preproduction units getting seeded next year in multiple applications. So there's definitely customer interest in that. So we're excited about that, and we need to do a good job with those initial launches and impacts that will ramp in '15, but we are definitely going into, we will have engines running in multiple end markets next year. One of the reasons why the company spent very well in terms of margin performance of the past few years has been the increasing exposure we have to high horsepower markets, and that includes the mining market. So I think as you look at over the longer term, you're going to see that becoming an increasingly prominent feature of the portfolio that Cummins participates in, and that's why we're making the type of investment we're making today.

question: I guess a follow-up to that question. If you were to look at North America kind of all of your off-highway businesses put together, obviously, there's a lot of moving parts, a lot of different segments, oil and gas in there, but there's construction, there's mining, everything, if you were to put that all together, would you expect that to be up in '15 or flat or down? What -- I guess what are you seeing in that regard?
answer: Down slightly overall. Oil and gas will be down 20% from Q1 levels. It will be down a little for the full year. Mining will be down a little bit for the year. Construction for us will be down. That doesn't leave many of the significant pieces, probably commercial marine will be about flat. So in aggregate, a little down. Parts will be parts growth to offset lower equipment sales, but lower single digit down, I would say, Alex.

question: I'm wondering if you folks can just flesh out for us the Power Gen expectations that you laid out for 2016, which is pretty good margin performance, in context of the sales decline. Maybe just help us understand where the cost savings are coming from. And how should we think about decremental margins if sales are at the low end of your sales range or another 5% to 10% lower? What levers would you be able to pull in that business?
answer: Jerry, this is Rich. Just a reminder on how -- on 2015, we initiated a lot of cost reduction towards the end of 2014. And in 2015, we realized 16% decremental margins, which is a little better than what our normal 25% that we would say. What we're committed to in 2016, actually, is to increase margins on reduced sales. And so probably 3 major areas, but 1 is the restructuring work that we kicked off before, we'll get a full year impact of that in 2015. The actions we took in Q4, for example the roughly a 7% professional headcount reduction was much heavier in the Power Gen Business. So it exceeded 10% in the Power Gen Business. Tom mentioned that some plants restructuring that we've done, that was all in the Power Generation Business. And again, we're looking to further actions in that area. So we feel confident, even with the lower sales levels, it will in fact increase the EBIT going forward in 2016 with those actions.

question: I've got a bunch of questions. And this one, I may -- we asked you on the call and I know it's showing through irrelevancy almost in Brazil, but I'm a little curious how you manage that business down '15 to '17? I don’t know if you'd give the total revenue number or not. Are you losing 10% margins there? Do you manage to stem it at breakeven? Like how do you manage such a volatile market? You guys are best in the business at this, I would like to hear what you did.
answer: Yes, but what we've been doing, and maybe we've not been so transparent about it, but there's been a number of restructuring actions over the last 3 or 4 years. It's almost every year. We've been reducing headcount, taking actions to get the cost structure in line with demand. The problem is here, Rob, demand just keeps growing there. So Brazil revenues now are probably less than 2% of total company revenue, just to give you a sense of the size for us just now. But one of the things, I think, the 4 business segments are really good at is working in a difficult market when revenues are down. So even Power Generation, which has been under enormous pressure for the last 2, 3, 4 years with declining market, last year, on lower sales, they managed to hold the decremental margins to around 15%. So lots of good work going on in restructuring. But is kind of masked, when your sales keep falling away, you're not really seeing the benefit once we get stabilization there, that's when I think they'll see better incrementals come through. And I think, giving a smaller point, Rob. We have got a lot of local content in Brazil. So the market's down, but our costs are downs also a lot. So that's helped people who are in important.

question: Yes, just going back to NA on-highway. Do you have any thoughts on kind of capacity impacts from the ELD mandate should it go through? And how that would look for production maybe next year, 2018, anything along those lines?
answer: I think at least most of the participants that I've heard from or indirectly through our business leaders indicate there's going to be some capacity impact from the implementation of the ELD regulations. There's also some speculation in the industry that the large and more sophisticated fleets are already complying with these regulations or implementing a lot of these practices. So it shouldn't be so disruptive to them. And our market share with the top 200 fleets is well north of our overall market share. So I think to the extent it favors the larger fleets and their more efficient operators, we're able to adapt in the light of any capacity constraints then. I'm hopeful there won't be any negative impact to Cummins at least, but I can't tell you exactly what's going to be the overall change in the industry. There's a general sense that there's going to be some capacity pressure, I think.

question: Yes, and not to nickel and dime you. Even with that cost on the startup, you're still implying decrementals over 40? I'm just trying to make sure -- I mean, is the inflation problems particular to components more than other segments?
answer: No, it's not. So again, just thinking through your view of our guidance. Again, as I've said kind of as an overview, we're taking a pretty conservative view of bad markets. And so I think the biggest opportunity we have in the Components business is that North American markets strengthen more and faster than what we have in our guidance, and you probably have a reasonable view about your opinion on that. So that would be one thing that you could take a look at if you wanted to. But again, our view is that we're going to continue to manage conservatively. We're going to continue to find ways to take costs out. So again, as you know, we are not satisfied with decremental margins of that level. We're not pleased with that. We are working hard to figure out how to make that less of an impact, but we're giving you the forecast based on what we think we understand how to do right now. We'll continue to work on decremental margins in that business. That's a very -- it's a very profitable and good business for Cummins, and we're going to continue to make it so.

question: Yes, can't get much lower than 0. I was reading that. What do you think about internal investment? One of the things we're exploring is whether increased technology, Digital factory, automation, cheapness of robotics, cheapness of really more digital systems and factory is leading to a higher return on internal investment versus -- M&A is not cheaper lately, right? So what's your opinion on that balance? And do you see that as becoming more favorable?
answer: Well our bias and our preference long-term is unchanged. There is always a safer bet to invest in what you know inside your business that go and acquire. It always is. And we've done really well on that over the last decade. And that's why our return on average net to assets has been north of 20% for all that period of time, even through the worst parts of the cycle. So you're always looking there first. The reason why we are kind of pivoting a little bit is that some of those markets, at least for the next few years, can still be fairly muted. But what -- we're always going to be looking to bring out new engines in the markets that we known -- that we know well today, that's always going to priority number one.

question: Pat, you talked about since the election, the sentiment may be being better. But if you look across your businesses in North America, are there any places you've seen actual order upticks yet in that period -- in this period since the election?
answer: So, I miss the second part. Any parts where --

question: Okay, got it. That's really helpful. And, I guess, my second question is just around China. So last quarter, you guys talked about a competitive pricing environment within China truck. I'm just curious if that's continued into the first quarter? Or if you've seen that eased?
answer: I don't think it's impacting our results right now. So that probably there hasn't been significant change at this point in time. Yes, most of that was related to market share acquisition by one OEM of the other that launched some new models, that we're trying to acquire. And with the new regulations that are requiring -- on overloading, that are requiring some fleets to actually purchase new trucks, our expectation is that pricing competition will ease. But frankly, we were even surprised by the size of the growth in the truck market in the first quarter as we were with the excavators. So we have some work to do to understand how well that's going to hold up and how pricing markets are just reflecting back on the first quarter. But right now, we expect the pricing to ease under the circumstances.

question: Okay, got it. And speaking of market share, I thought maybe you could comment on customer response to the new Hedgehog engine. I guess are you -- and are you starting to see share gains relative to some of your competitors like Cat?
answer: Yes. So the Hedgehog product, so let me quickly set this up. And so this is the strongest high-speed diesel engine out in the industry. So we launched a 16-cylinder, 95-liter version of this product a couple of years ago. The launch markets were power generation, the rail market with locomotive applications, and then the marine space. So in those 3 markets, we've launched the product. And the customer feedback has been quite spectacular on all 3 fronts. Adoption cycles are slightly different because the equipment build cycles and design cycles are a little bit different. I mean, for example, we are winning a very large share, for example, of airport power generation sites or large global data centers. And the data center space right now is extremely hot in most regions of the world. So on the power gen side, the power density and the capability of the product has been extremely well received. And we've taken quite a bit of market share there. On the rail side, again we've just got a partnership with Siemens and also the end user, some of the locomotives are going into service as we speak. So we've worked on the product for 2 years. They're now in revenue service in California. And we're soon going to go into service in Florida and Michigan as well. And it's been amazing. The customer, even the train operators, are looking at the equipment and say, "Is it running?" Because it's so quiet compared to previous equipment. So we think that the end user adoption between the fact that it's extremely clean compared to legacy product, very fuel-efficient and from a noise level, just a totally next-generation product, I think we'll continue to take market share. I think that the reception has been really, really good. And then on the marine space right now, it's a tough time to show up with a very new product like that because there's not so much build activity to begin with. So again, the applications that we've placed it into, we just had a phone call with the captain, there's one boat on the coast of Angola. And we had a conversation, and the captain has been running the equipment now for 500, 600 hours, super happy with the performance and the fuel economy and everything. I think in that space, the adoption is going to be a bit more challenging just because the general build activity at the moment is a bit depressed.

question: The European truck market, you're not as large a player, but you have some of your supply agreements on components of these so-called fuel injectors. Can you give us a little feel? The European market's been maybe a little more resilient than I would have thought. Can you give us your perspective?
answer: Yes, so Europe had a good year, obviously, last year. And if we look into this year, we think it's going to be relatively flat. It could be, at a -- historically, at pretty good levels. So we don't see any indication that there's going to be a big pullback, so that market continues to be strong for us.

question: Yes, we see dealer inventory is below. I mean, it's below historical averages, but I don't think -- it's low, but you're saying it went from an impediment to at least now it's -- it's a slight net positive, it's not that low yet, but at least it's in the right direction.
answer: And it is also, depending on who it is, which OEM it is. Some OEMs have a little bit more than others, and so they're trying to -- some of them called the shots right early and others did not at that time and so there is a little bit of a glut in 1 or 2 going into this [ together or separately ].

question: So we'll have $1.50 of tailwind in 2019 just to wake up on January 1?
answer: Yes. It's just a point. I'm not trying to be flippant here, so I apologize for that. It was very, very disappointing with the [ hardware ] issue. But I think the company stepped up and dealt with it in the right way. And we're glad it's now behind us financially.

question: So with that, thank you very much, Mark. I guess, we'll, sort of, kick off. Lots of concerns, debate on the North American heavy-duty truck cycle, the longevity of it, the cancellation rates we saw sort of last month. So can you talk about sort of your view of the heavy-duty truck market, the things that you're watching to sort of monitor whether or not we're at peak, close to peak or however you want to define it?
answer: Yes, so we started asking a lot more questions of our big fleet customers, probably 5 or 6 months ago, when we're seeing really high order rates, 45,000, 50,000 orders a month, and the question we had at that time was, really -- were there really any more orders left to come. And what we heard, Jamie, from some of the big fleets is that still several of them had not really placed significant orders for this year at that point in time. So it felt like confidence from the fleets was still pretty strong, but like everything, it's -- it really is all about the confidence going forward, so we have not detected a change in tone at this point in time from customers. Obviously, we know, the order rates are extraordinarily high, and at some point, they are going to taper off. We're sitting here with a all-time record industry backlog, and that's why Cummins and probably some of our really important customers are touting pretty high confidence into the first half of the year. But I mean theoretically, we've got a backlog that takes the industry beyond that, but it's really going to be about confidence in the U.S. economy. As we look across more segments of our business in North America, they look pretty strong right now. There is -- in the pocket, we're not in the passenger car business, but obviously, sales are starting to slow there. But if we look at pickup truck demand, very strong; construction equipment, strong; power generation, positive; mining, still positive. So for now, you know, North America, which is our largest market, we're pretty positive of, but we got to keep that confidence in the U.S. economy going. I haven't seen a big change in sentiment.

question: Okay. So shifting -- sorry, to market share -- sorry, on -- within North America on heavy-duty side, that's been trending probably at the higher end of what your forecast has been. So what have been the drivers behind that? I'm assuming it's more constraints from your customers and so you're gaining incidental market share, is it that? Or is it something different and is that a sustainable level, assuming the market starts to deteriorate?
answer: So I think we have 2 dynamics going on really in the market. One, what do the fleets want? What do those truck fleets want? And the feedback we're getting is that our ISX 15 liter engine is performing incredibly well, so we feel we're competing really well. Therefore, the demand from the end-users is high. Yes, there'll always be situations, we have the -- typically the most flexible, the additional capacity in the industry. So yes, people can push more orders to us when things get tight, but at the same time, the fleets have got to want -- have to want those engines. So, yes, we've seen in the past in peak cycles our share tends to move up. When gets really tough, the OEMs will try and prioritize their own production. But I think bottom line is, we feel really, really good about competitiveness of 15 liter. Despite these debates, Jamie, we've been having since, I have known you, over the last 10 years, we are now producing an all-time record number of 15-liter engines today in our Jamestown Plant and I think we could sell a few more from this. I think we're bullish, we've got the discontinuation of 1 engine family this year and the replacement engine is going to ramp up slowly, so that's a little bit of noise in the numbers, but it doesn't even show up until that those truck sales happen next year, but you could see a little bit of change in the numbers, but I think the underlying demand is very, very, very strong.

question: I did want to ask you one other question before I forget around the light-duty market. You -- it's a business that did very well for you in 2012, really with one product or one engine going to one customer. But we've heard rumblings about other potential customers. And so you don't -- you didn't mention that as a potential upside. Why couldn't that be a big potential upside in that particular business?
answer: I think it could. I mean we clearly have an engine that's pretty much ready. Again, for those who don't know the history, we're developing this engine there for a number of years. We had an agreement with the old Chrysler before they went to bankruptcy. When they came out, they did not want the engine the same deal that we agreed with the previous version. So they went down a different path. There are people interested in the engine. So all investments effective made.  The facility is ready, the technology is ready, and there is a fair amount of investment -- of interest. I can't be more specific -- I'd like to be more specific. I just can't be more specific just now as to where we are in discussions with those parties at the moment. I'd just like to add, though, it wasn't clear there, Andy, if you were talking about the North American market. We've invested heavily in light-duty engines in China with our partner on Foton. We're also selling light-duty engines into Brazil and into Russia. So there is growing demand for light-duty engines generally, so that's definitely an area that we're focusing a lot in the company.

question: First, Mark, you guys touch a lot of different markets. Could you give a regional demand assessment? I'm trying to understand if China was a V-shaped improvement through mid-April and how you view the prospects for other regions, including North America? So have you seen activity improve sequentially from mid-April or the short-term demand recovery look more L-shaped in the non-China markets?
answer:
Okay. Good morning, everybody. I'll do my best, Andy. I'd say China is unique. I definitely would not want to try and extrapolate what's going on in China only because there's no data to support extrapolation. So hopefully, that's very clear to everybody. 
I'm not trying to overexcite people but as you've seen, maybe from some of the commentary from the passenger car participants, we've seen a very similar story in our business in that there's been a rapid rebound in truck demand, particularly heavy- and medium-duty trucks, which, of course, is our core market. And quite frankly, the pace of rebound has shocked us. So we've gone from, in weeks of February and March, hardly making any engines to making all-time record high numbers of engines for the heavy- and medium-duty truck market in April. So that's remarkable. 
The industry data, I'm not sure if it's fully released yet for all the segments, but we have access to data that says year-to-date heavy- and medium-duty truck market is flat year-over-year. So we've had a really strong rebound in industry-wide sales in April, and as I said, record production of engines for the heavy- and medium-duty segment in April. 
So that's -- we're not building to stock. We're building to OEM orders. The multimillion/billion-dollar question is what happens as we get through this recovery period and how long does this level of demand sustain? It's not uniform across all end markets, Andy. As you said, we touch various end markets. So we did see a rebound pretty much in most segments in April in China, but the year-to-date data on excavators and light-duty trucks, in particular, is not as good as heavy- and medium-duty truck. 
So yes, that's kind of the shining light. The question, I guess, remains how long does a battery stay on and how long does the light keeps shining that strongly in China? We don't have good visibility into what happens even in Q3 at this point in time. We're typically working on 2-week lead times. So that is the global anomaly at this point in time. 
I think for the rest of the world or most of the rest of the world, we're just trying to -- the industries are trying to -- I should add one thing, Andy. I think what's gone on in China has really demonstrated the flexibility of the Cummins supply chain. So going from close to 0 to all-time record in a matter of a few weeks demonstrates kind of the expertise of our people in really ramping up. And often, that's what our customers rely on. We have the most flexible supply chain in the industry, and so we've responded well. It's not always been pretty, but we've been able to keep up with this kind of record demand. 
Outside of China, we're kind of -- everybody's limping back to work, and so customers in various phases of opening up their operations. So I think there was -- maybe not everybody who follows our industry was entirely clear, the extent to which our customers and suppliers shut down in April. But we were talking 50%, 60%, 70% in some weeks of the customer locations that we shipped to were closed. So April is -- hopefully is an anomaly in history in terms of what happened in our industry, not just at Cummins. 
So what we're trying to deal with in terms of assessing the environment is -- going forward is, one, at what rate and pace are customers starting up. It appears to us as a general average statement, they're starting up at lower rates of production than they -- from which they descended in mid- to late-March. And then the question is how well can that global supply chain respond because it's faced a number of shocks in China, then we've had -- India is a big source of component supply for the world, India's shut down. So we're going through those gyrations. 
On top of that, as you know, we face a wave of, quite frankly, sad economic data that's not surprising when a massive chunk of the world's economy is being shut down. So truck orders, you're obviously very familiar with, Andy, in North America, general economic data is weak, but that's to be expected. I think we've got to wait for more data points to give us confidence about what happens from hereon in. 
Obviously, in the U.S., the rate of increase in unemployment and the knock-on effect's probably the biggest concern. And then we know that truck fleet age isn't -- is relatively young relative to prior years, has been a fairly strong buying cycle in U.S. construction. So we think a reasonable waiting period from customers before they get back on the accelerator even when the economic data starts to clear, we could be faced with an extended period of uncertainty about when demand starts to pick up again from the end users.

question: Okay. Great. Well, James, thank you so much for joining us today, and thank you to everyone on the line. I really appreciate your time, and good luck with the rest of your meetings today.
answer: Great. Thanks so much.

question: Maybe, Jack, can you kind of give us a little bit more context in terms of the magnitude of the inventory build you're seeing in China? How much happened in kind of first quarter? Is that continuing to build in the second quarter? And maybe remind us for context, during prior emissions changes in China or some of the regions that have already gone to NS VI, kind of what you saw just so we can kind of put that into context.
answer:
Yes. So generally speaking, if we look back over the past couple of years, we've seen inventory levels, hover between kind of 150,000 to 200,000 units across the major OEMs kind of the top 8 to 10. That has started to tick up, I would say, at the back end of 2020 and now is hovering in the close to 300,000 as we've moved through the beginning of this year. And so that, coupled with just normal kind of prebuy dynamics and what we generally see is a slow momentum out of the gate when there's a new regulation, is leading us to believe that, again, first half will be quite strong and second half will taper off a bit as the OEMs need to work through these inventory levels. 
And generally speaking, end users will be a little hesitant out of the gate to try out the new technology, which will be a bit more expensive due to the content increase.
We have seen various regions, like I mentioned earlier, pushed back some of the registrations for end users when they can register a new vehicle and allow a little bit more of a grace period from when they can do that. And so basically, what that does is allow production to occur basically right up until the implementation of the new standard and then registration can continue on for a period of time thereafter. So for us, the revenue impact is that we'll, again, see a lot more activity in the first half of the year and then the OEMs will again liquidate their inventory and realize their revenue kind of over the back end of this quarter and into Q3.

question: I think in a former life you sat on the M&A team and worked on the Hydrogenics deal, but can you talk a little bit about some of the disruptors that are -- the smaller disruptors that are out there in the hydrogen space and in electric that are trying to get into the commercial vehicle market? What are some of the challenges that they're facing relative to a brand that is housed within Cummins?
answer:
Yes. So I think a couple of things that we have an advantage on. One is our application knowledge. We continue to have significant experience both within our distribution business as well as in our new power and our engine business on how these various applications work, which is something that we can leverage regardless of what technology is being adopted and something that we work closely with our customers on, particularly at the more regional OEM level. We don't always have that capability in-house. 
That distribution channel also helps us sell and service the units in the field, and we feel like that will continue to be a really important strategic advantage that we can bring to the table, which is really hard to replicate for a new start-up in the field.
And then finally, I think some of the staying power, if you will, or long-term benefits that Cummins can provide have helped us as we've navigated some of these new commercial partnerships and equity partnerships. We have got a long proven history of a significant portfolio of joint ventures and other commercial partnerships, which I think give some of these larger entities comfort that we'll be a good partner for the long term. We will continue to invest in these spaces and be there for the long term. And there's perhaps greater certainty if you partner with Cummins than some others in the field. 
And so we're really optimistic about what we've got today from a technology standpoint. We will continue to invest to improve that as we move into next new-generation products. And we feel like our ability to then bring that technology to these partners who in turn can bring market access and volume creates a really compelling win-win to help us continue to build that business.

question: If I'm correct, they don't guarantee you anything on new programs or increased content on current ones. But do you have any expectations on that? Are you hearing anything from your peers about participating too?
answer: Well, as a matter of fact, we are -- we did build our merchant operations facility in support of Boeing. And this is part of that. When we provide them the capability, almost a build-it-and-they-will-come perspective. They are looking at us as a more viable, let's call it a subcontractor vendor in a local area. And you're right, they don't promise you an increased content or share, but you certainly get a new peak at opportunities that where -- we would not have had prior to that. And it gives us the opportunity to compete. And we do very well in that regard. So we anticipate picking up new top line as a result of our participation. That's the whole thing that Boeing is going after.

answer: Yes. I was reading some of those same articles of recent, and it looks more on the construction side. And some that are late -- I mean, some of the projects are late, however. And overruns, I read about those as well, but what I also read was that they are making progress. I think that there are only 2 that are active today, but that they are actually making progress.
