question: So Steve, I like that -- I like the consolidation and innovation theme. It's pretty catching and pretty applicable to you all. Can you talk a little bit more on the innovation side of things? Where can you go from here? I mean, obviously, longer laterals are sort of the, I guess, I'll say the layup. But when you look at just in sort of the proppant loading, stage spacing, where do you think you could go from where we're at today?
answer: Well, I think on the -- like on the completion side, as we mentioned before, we've started doing bigger frac jobs and higher proppant loadings. We're not quite ready to announce any revisions to our type curves, but I would expect that we'll have an update by the next call. We just want to get a little more data there. And we're expanding that to -- we're now testing even higher proppant loads. That will take some more time to conclude how much or if there's a benefit there, but we continue to experiment and look for better ways on the completion side. I would say our innovations are solely focused on drilling and completion activities, though. And a couple of areas that we're doing a lot of work in are kind of more on the logistical side. So we're doing a lot of operations research kind of work on our rig scheduling and our frac scheduling and how we move and transport water. And what we're finding through some pretty advanced modeling is our previous assumptions about what was optimum turn out to be pretty far off. And the conclusions from these models really aren't intuitive. Very difficult for a human being to look at spreadsheet and come up with the optimum schedule. So we're just starting that kind of work. We think the applicability to our business could be pretty widespread and potentially pretty dramatic in terms of lowering our unit operating cost. So a lot of work happening in that area. It'll take some time, but we're pretty excited about it.

question: Can you give us a little bit more color on the synergies plan and implementing the synergies from the Rice transaction over the course of -- or over 2018, just the areas of focus and potential benefits here now relative to where you expect to be at the end of the year?
answer: Yes. So Brian, so we announced 2 primary synergies that drove the deal, one on the G&A side. We are at or a little bit ahead of the plan that delivered on that synergy. So I think the annual savings is going to be a bit better than we anticipated. Yes, what we had said was we expected about $100 million of annual G&A savings or overhead savings. And we think that number is going to be more like $110 million or maybe a little more than that for 2018. And on the capital savings, the model assumed 12,000-foot laterals in the acquisition area. And we now expect to average 13,600 feet. So that's a pretty dramatic acceleration of those synergies. And I don't have the PV benefit of that difference with me, but it's... It's several hundred million dollars higher.

question: Got it, got it. And then you had mentioned that -- and I guess your average type curves is about 2.4 Bcf per 1,000 foot, and then '19 is 2.6 at 880. Did I hear that right? Is there a bit of high grading going on in '19? Or is there a reason why that's above the average?
answer: Right, so the 2.4 has been our historical average, which was on narrower well spacing. So now in 2019, we're moving to 880-foot well spacing on average. And we will pump slightly larger frac jobs, and that drives the higher recoveries.

question: Given some of the issues that you highlight earlier around the West Virginia and the limited activity that's planned for the region in 2019, what's your appetite for carving off some of that acreage to offset the land spending for bolt-ons in Southwest PA? It seems like it could be a pretty easy way to boost free cash flow while further high-grading your acreage.
answer: We're always willing to consider selling acreage that's further back in the drilling queue. If somebody is willing to pay us more than what we think it's worth in our portfolio, so we're always open-minded about that. I would caution, however, that there's not a long list of buyers for acreage out there right now, given where gas prices are and the shape of some companies' balance sheets. So while we're always open-minded about that, I would caution about too much optimism in terms of available buyers.

question: Yes, it does. And then my follow-up is a little bit more on color on the decision to bring your shut-in production back online and why -- to do that now at what seems to be similar prices as what was experienced in the second quarter? Or was it that you expected that the second quarter could be potentially even worse than it was?
answer:
Yes. So Brian, we -- the goal for us was to really take the extra production and really move it out into future periods. I think if you remember, we were running nicely ahead in the first quarter. And so our goal was really to just to take the excess production, keep our production relatively flat with 2019 and get the benefit of, in future periods, of shutting in production.
So we are very, very hedged. And so even bringing it back, we're very well hedged and not impacted from bringing it back. Having said that though, you're right, the economics still like shutting in production could be worthwhile, and that's something we'll look at and see if we decide we want to shut in more production that -- in sort of, call it, the late either summer or in the fall.

question: Okay, clear enough. Appreciate that. And I guess -- go ahead, sorry.
answer: I was just going to say, customers on the ACP line, they were signing up for over $1.50 of fees. And so I mean, these costs would have been passed through to their customers. I mean these are utilities. So to be able to have the opportunity to pass-through $0.77 versus $1.50 is ultimately better for the consumers as well. So I mean that's one of the things that's underpinning why we believe we can get this done at cost.

question: Yes. It's great to hear. And then [indiscernible] tight capacity but the other. Then my thought is, again, given where gas prices are, obviously, returns are fantastic. Are you -- do you weigh like when you and Dave were looking at it, is there -- I guess sort of a 2-part question, are there opportunities to roll in, I don't know, either bolt-ons or some bigger deals? And if so, is it just simply comparing that to -- you have [ ample acreage ], no question, being the largest gas player. Is it just simply a comparison of what the deal price looks like maybe on PDPs or however you want to value them versus what's your organic growth to be?
answer: Yes, Neal. So I think anything -- any asset you look at, I think you want to make sure you're getting quality. So we definitely compare asset quality versus ours. I think you look at Alta, the cost structure  that asset base did, it lowered our cost structure of this company, lowered our breakevens by over $0.05. So that's one consideration. But I mean, at the end of the day, everything we do on M&A is going to be. It's got to be more accretive than buying back our stock, and that's the ultimate decision.

question: Okay. Bob, free cash flow obviously very strong last year, strong this quarter. Can you just give us a sense -- I know you talked about it coming in, in line or better than net income this year, but can you give us a sense kind of the big moving pieces, working capital, cash taxes, kind of how those look for the -- what you're thinking about for the full year?
answer: Yes, that's a great question, David. I will say that one area of focus that we are looking at intensely right now is inventory. That's one of the reasons why I mentioned it in my comments. And we see some good opportunities there, along with working capital in total. And we continue to focus on maintaining our historic strong metrics in free cash flow and increasing them dramatically. But our receivables capabilities are strong. We continue to have good payment patterns there. Inventory is an area that we need to focus on. Payables is an area we're looking at in conjunction with our strategic sourcing activities. And we think we've got opportunities in each of those areas. I'll add one -- let me just add one comment there. As I went around, the cash flow in this business is very strong, so there's been probably more focus on margins, costs. But we are going to focus on improving our cash flow performance. I guess, harnessing it, because it is very good. But one other thing I've noted is that we've had some delinquencies with customers in our -- well, we have some great operational performance. Souriau just got I think, what, the seventh in a row Best Supplier at Airbus for on-time delivery performance, but we've got some others that we've impacted customers. And very clear, my message out to them was, we will not impact our customers, we have to be best-in-class. And so I think some of this inventory build might have been a little buffering to make sure that we're meeting our delivery commitments, but we are definitely going to be using operational excellence to drive that back down, to get our terms -- get our turns to improve, because I don't -- they're not where they need to be at all in my mind.

question: Okay. Okay, that's helpful. And then what about if you can comment how you guys -- into your strategic planning or what the status is of Boeing's Partnering for Success initiative, what you guys are seeing there on some of your key programs and product lines?
answer: Well, we're working very closely. They're one of our biggest customers, and so we're working real closely with them. I luckily got some experience with Partnering for Success at Goodrich and at UTC and now here, the -- we're trying to work with some basic philosophies of how can we jointly go take cost out. They have supported some of our integration moves. And in consideration for that, we've shared some of the savings where they've helped support us. We're looking at opportunities where we can drive volume improvements or engineering change improvements. So it's something that we have to go work with them on. I think today, we're not done with them yet. We have some businesses that I think are -- I would say that they've wrapped up and they've done what they can do. We've got some others that are still making proposals, and we have -- just in the last couple of months, we've had a number of meetings with them. I've gone up there and met with them personally to talk about the direction of the company and to see what we can do to work closely together. So we're engaged with them, but we don't have a final solution set yet. But we're sure working on it. And we've got that with other customers. It's pretty typical with some of the big primes, where we're trying to work with them on how we can drive performance and help share it with them. I will say this: that's nothing new from what I've seen. And I've told my team we just -- we've got to be competitive in the marketplace and continually take cost out of our business. And there's an expectation that we're going to have to be competitive in the marketplace and probably share some of that with our customer. So that's something that I think is just a given in this industry, and we're going to become really good at taking out cost and hopefully put more of that to our margin improvement than we give away.

question: You talked about R&D being roughly 5%. What's in there today? And where do you see directing? I mean, are there top -- are the top 5 programs accounting for 20% of the spending? Or is it very evenly spread at the moment, Curtis?
answer: Yes. We have right around -- it tapers down from 5, and most of that, however, is just visibility. I think 5 is a good placeholder, and that's what we've got in going forward. I think as our sales build up in the out-years, it may tick slightly under 5, at 4.9 or something like that. But it's roughly 5. And there is a pretty good mix. Frank's business spends the lion's share of it. CMC spends a big -- probably the largest chunk in big programs. Alain's got some on the sensor side. So it is a longer cycle pieces. Some of our businesses, even saying that, Greg's got some programs at CMC where we get funded by the customer. So that is -- the 5% is a net 5%. I think if you looked at gross, Bob, with customer funded, it would be... 6%, 7%, 8%. Yes, 6%, 7%, 8% and then you net down where we get funded. It varies. Al's group has probably the least amount of R&D. And actually, and I applaud him for it, we went and tweaked his numbers up. His guys said we were down in the lower 1%, 2%. And it was like, let's allocate some money there because we should be able to go drive -- invest in some of the ordinance programs, there are some technologies there that we want to go invest, and I think that's prudent.

question: Okay. A lot of moving pieces there, just reason for caution, okay. And then just wondering, just on the cash flow side. Can you give us a sense of what you expect D&A to be in fiscal '15 and that if you expect working capital to grow in fiscal '15 or not?
answer: Yes, Peter, and those are 2 very different questions. We'd expect depreciation, amortization to be approximately the same level as '14, which is, give or take, around $115 million to $117 million. That, of course, is on a same-store business. As you know, from our previous announcement, we're looking to close the acquisition of Barco sometime during the year. That will certainly increase the amortization of intangible assets. We currently don't have -- we don't have an assessment on that. But same-store sales, we're looking in and around that range. Working capital, as we've talked about in the past and I think I'll let Curtis talk to it, is one of our key strategic initiatives. In fact, it's one of our initiatives on our IC plans and the like. And we expect to see progress in working capital metrics. Curtis, you want to make a few comments? Yes, I think, overall, working capital climbed in the year, and I think Bob, we ended up back -- we just reviewed this with the board. We ended up kind of back at the same levels, but we did have some build. I did press the team to say we've got to get our delivery performance. I'd mentioned this before. We had a number of contracts where we were not helping our customers. And I -- that's -- I do not like doing that. That's what we're here to do, is to help support our commitments that we've made. So we did build up some safety stock to support customer demands and commitments. We've also had a little bit of working capital buildup as we moved our projects. Some of these accelerated integration projects were moving from one facility to another, so we've seen some buildup there. We're starting to peel that back down. We have a very specific program to go look at working capital. As Bob mentioned, we just got approval for a new IC structure that ties a number of the specific initiatives that we have. We've tied people's IC to that, and one of those is in improvement in working capital. And working with our lean -- the E3 [ph], excellence -- the Esterline Enterprise Excellence. We're going to be going in the first quarter and rolling out a program that I'm familiar with before that really slices and dices inventory and ages it and looks at ordering practices across the businesses, and so we're going to be rolling that out. So again, that's a big system. You got to look at the -- you got to look at turning a lot of dials before the sausage comes out of the end, but I expect it to get better, and it is. Just one comment on Barco. Bob mentioned that it -- I think he probably noted. We've announced Barco. None of our numbers here include Barco, and so when we do -- when we get to that point, it's progressing well, no showstoppers. We're in final negotiations with them. We will come out and give update guidance when that happens.

question: Okay. And then just on the aftermarket, mid-single digit growth. I mean, it seems like there's still a lot of puts and takes to that market. I mean, you seem pretty confident in that view. I mean, are you seeing any different trends among your customers there? I mean, it just seems like, depending on platform and engine exposure, that the growth has been pretty volatile, but I mean do you have good line of sight into that forecast?
answer: We think we do. Again, we're off of a lower base. We did have some of the pressure from some of the more reliable sensors on the engine side. And I believe a couple of our engine guys, specifically Rolls, did some inventory balancing between their shops. So that did have some pressure, but that was mostly in '14 and early '15. So I think that's why we did see a little bit of rebound there. So we feel more confident in that piece of it. On the switch side, we did see a little softness on some of the aftermarket there on the commercial side but some strength on the military side. So again, we've done a -- I think, a fair job of looking at it and think that we can support those kind of growth rates. But it is volatile. I mean, you don't -- that is -- I get a weekly report on that stuff and it's -- if you looked at the trend, it is up and down. Every -- it's a noisy line. But we think that we have a pretty good line of sight on the trends.

question: Right. I mean, the euro or the pound, or -- I get that, but I meant relative to the dollar. And I get the mix or the cost structure is largely in Canada. Just to go to DAT for a moment, Curtis. How have you found the organizations fit together? And can you point to either some synergies? Or as you look at the DAT business going forward, is it starting to meet the plan that you've laid out at the time you acquired the business?
answer: Yes, very good question, Howard. Yes, it is. I will say that the integration effort has been a little more time consuming and a little more costly. We did have to put in a new ERP system and some beefed up IT infrastructure in addition to some catch-up work on compliance. We have a couple really good milestones this quarter. We had the actual State Department went over to Belgium. They're visiting 5 of our sites. Visits concluded in this last quarter and the reports were the DAT guys were in trouble, but they are, like, best-in-class now. So some great progress there. We've had to add some additional resources, but we're getting over the hump there. Same thing with the IT systems. But a couple of comments I'll make about DAT, really good people. Two of their individuals now are leading sales efforts, one for our ECCS segment and one for Avionics, so a great team there. The management team is gelling very well, so very strong people. We are identifying -- we just had our strategic plan with those guys. We are identifying a number of incremental opportunities where Avionics -- you know CMC didn't have a foot in the door, the DAT people are pulling them along and vice versa. We're working on some rationalization of the R&D costs. We're making progress on moving the facilities from Duluth up into Everett. So again, good progress so far. We probably have had a little heavier load on some of the integration efforts, but we're making very solid progress.

question: I wanted to -- hey guys, I wanted to -- Curtis, since we last saw you a couple of months ago, any different view on the macro, particularly on the commercial OE cycle? Do you feel that it's maybe strengthening here, weakening? Obviously, Boeing cut the 777 in the interim, but how do you feel?
answer: Pretty much the same way, Rob. The 777's down a little bit. We've seen some pressure obviously on A380. We keep watching what they're going to do on narrow-body rates. But I don't see any -- since we talked, I don't see any big difference.

question: Can you guys talk a little bit more about the order activity, the $466 million in orders? While I understand that the year-over-year comparison, it is still below your bookings, so you're getting a little bit of a decline in the backlog. So just what are you seeing in terms of order activity? And then more specifically, how about some of the international defense opportunities like the avionics that you've been going after in the past?
answer: Yes, again, some of those things are lumpy. We've got some simulation orders. Again, it's in our displays business that comes under avionics. We do have some new cockpit opportunities that we're looking at and there's a pretty long list of them that can move the needle. We're expecting, knock on wood, to get some of these. We had a few of the nuclear orders come through but those are pretty sizable from our U.K. business and we're expecting some of that activity to happen later in the year. There are some orders supporting, I think, some Turkish business that, I think, the connection folks are out chasing. So there's a couple -- there's some nice activity internationally and some larger orders that we feel pretty comfortable about. But it is a little bit lumpier than normal.

question: I want to ask you about pork. Obviously, that's been spiking only a bit recently, and you've mentioned the headwinds in your release along with the idea of mitigating that, which you've done very successfully in the past. Can you just remind us a little bit of how you managed to keep that, the sow inflation from materially impacting you previously? And then what those plans look like going forward?
answer: This is Steve Davis. Well, first -- and we've been talking about this for couple of years now -- as we grow our side dish business, and we think that with the higher sow prices, you'll probably see flat to slower growth consumption on the sausage side of the business, where the side dish business continues to grow. Couple that with vertical integration as a result of the acquisition with Kettle Creations, that should put us in a more favorable margin situation than we have been historically on that side of the business. And then Paul can talk to you about some of the things that we've done within products to not just offset the sow cost, but just to improve overall productivity of which sow cost does impact the profitability. Yes, so Will, one of the things that -- if you think about it, we have sort of medium and then longer-term things that we do to help us manage that sow cost. And so I talked a little bit about it in my prepared remarks, where we look at trade spending. And so trade spending is sort of the offset the sow cost. And as sow cost moves, we move trade spending to make sure that we're still controlling for the impact on the bottom line. And then over the longer term, we have really our efficiency initiatives that we're using to drive that. So we have what we call a lean manufacturing. We internally call it the GEAR Program, but we have a lean manufacturing process that we're trying to squeeze, excuse me, efficiencies out of the work that we are doing in our plants. And so we've been applying that over time, and you've seen us make changes to our plant network, for example, but we've also made a lot of efficiency improvements and capital investments that help us continuously drive efficiency in the facility. So we're constantly trying to offset this to the best we can, as well as diversify the product line.

question: Okay. And then looking at product mix within your restaurants, and you know that moving towards more tiered pricing, et cetera, more add-ons. Can you talk about -- and you hit on little bit of this earlier, but what you're seeing in your menu mix now or even maybe from customer feedback that led you to say, "This is route we need to go as far as putting more tiered pricing, and maybe some lower entry points, " et cetera, and then also maybe what that menu mixes looks like?
answer: Well, I think the insight is when budgets are the tight, people want certainty. And it doesn't matter if it's the restaurant dining, casual dining, family dining, pizza business, $10 seems to be a magical price point for everybody. So as long as you can stay under that $10 price point and sometimes include a beverage, that's the one thing that $7.99 does, is people will just want the $7.99 offering and they want to tack a beverage on, you know you are going to stay under $10. So as we were looking at our menu, we noticed we -- whether it was the half a sandwich and soup or whether it's the Rise & Shine or whether it's the Farmer's Choice Breakfast, which is a bundle of pancakes and meat and eggs, people are looking for more price certainty. So when we were doing the $6.99 and doing add-ons, it's sometimes hard to get the price certainty when you add multiple items on. So now what we've done is we've made it easier for the people to stay under that $10 price point. And for those people who define value as more food for the dollars, I mean, we sell a lot of the 3-course $9.99 dinners.  But if $9.99 is too steep, and you still want to get something at Bob Evans, you get a great meal and still add a beverage, you can do it for less than $10, which is kind of around everybody's guest check and casual and family dining.

question: My question is really to primarily the gross margin. Mark, what do you believe is the potential gross margin benefit of shifting menu mix to higher-margin breakfast items?
answer: Again, I think what we've targeted internally is somewhere in the 100 basis point shift as a result of shifting mix.

question: Any way you can give a little bit of detail as to how much lower, so -- I mean, it could have been a positive for -- helps to strip out what the true sort of margin is x that one project.
answer: I would have to check on it, but... It's probably a couple of 100 basis points on our margin, Gerry.

question: Okay. And none of that -- was that -- any of that the semiconductor job or was that all...
answer: It was all just every day business. It wasn't semiconductor at all. That's mostly going in the second quarter.

question: What the dollar value that, that would cost?
answer: In the $7 million range for next year's investment for this facility.

question: So I wanted to start kind of talking about on the guide for DynaEnergetics. And as I start to think about maybe the fourth quarter and into 2019, hearing customers, hearing peers and what they're talking about, I mean, one specifically said that the customer may even take breaks before Thanksgiving. When you look at the guidance, I would've expected a larger step-down. What might be you guys seeing differently than some of the other service customers out there?
answer: I think that our revenue is spread over more basins, and so we're less dependent upon the Permian. And we are seeing an increase in systems in the market versus components. And it's those 2 things, Ed.

question: I certainly get that, that, I mean, obviously, it's sort of dropship. But I was just curious if they actually gave you a little bit more inside look into their completion schedules, so if you had a little bit more visibility as to what they were planning. That's all, so --
answer: Well, we prefer to partner, and we're not trying to be all things to all people, but we want to make sure that we're all things to our customers that are doing business with us. And so we get insight to their activity; however, the ordering is very close to the consumption of our perforating guns.

question: Final one for me, Mike, if you don't mind, the SG&A for Q3, $17.5 million looks a little high. Can you talk about maybe what's going into that, embedded in that number? I mean, is there a catch-up on compensation or something like that?
answer: We've got some of that, but it's primarily just investing in some of the patents that we're building out in our portfolio of products that are going to be rolling out over the next several years. So we're investing in that, as well as continuing the sales and marketing efforts on the new products that we have introduced.

question: On that front -- and I didn't want to imply that you were chasing price components. But go ahead, I'm sorry.
answer: Well, we're not trying to be all things to all people. We're trying to be all things to a handful of people where we align culturally. And we're focused on creating value for the E&P and optimizing the ecosystem. And so they're -- we're going after the more technologically focused, total cost-focused companies who also value safety, reliability, the actual product performance and companies that are doing the right thing from an ESG standpoint. And so it's -- we're not trying to be all things to all people. We're trying to be the best in our area and associated with the best.

question: Okay. Okay. The other thing, we've seen some consolidation on the wire line front. And I was just kind of curious about how you're thinking about the impact of some of that consolidation on your business, right? Because we're thinking about maybe they get better pricing, which is good for you, but then I think at least one of the deals, there's a perf business which came with it. And I'm just trying to think about how the landscape is evolving and how that plays into DynaEnergetics' share and growth as we move forward.
answer:
We -- Stephen, we fully expect or expected the consolidation to begin taking place in this year. The consolidation is required or needed. And in addition to consolidation, there will be attrition and rationalization of some of the supply in the wire line service market. And that's healthy for the industry. It's healthy for our company. And so we're pleased to see it happen.
And regarding the -- I think there were 2 acquisitions, public company in the second quarter or were recently announced. And those companies use our products or have used our products. And so we're encouraged by the strengthening of that business, quite frankly.

question: Okay. That's fair. And then moving over to NobelClad. So the -- certainly, the back -- excluding the increased metal prices and the supply chain issues around key raw materials, the demand backdrop is setting up nicely for you guys with the strength in chemicals and petrochems and all the end markets that use your materials. How do you look at it over the next -- the second half, it sounds like it's going to get better. But into '23, '24, in terms of some -- finally getting some project growth through the system.
answer: Yes. I think when we look at this year, we're seeing mostly the price of metals entering into potentially higher revenue. And it -- there are large projects that are long cycle and when we book things in the second half of this year, they fall into next year. And so right now, we're working our backlog for the balance of this year, mostly. And we think the back half of the year will be up over the first half of the year and in the 8% to 10% range, but it's mostly pricing. And then we see -- we're not giving guidance yet for the back half, let alone for '23 and '24, but we'll start to see the projects get layered in for '23 and '24.

question: You just led into the next question. I've heard a lot about re-fracking. Obviously, it's an important part to the industry. Where do you guys, where are you with that? And are you seeing an increase in re-fracks?
answer: Re-fracks are maybe 3%, 4% of well completion programs today. Growing, but from a very small base. We historically haven't differentiated between perforating a new well or perforating an existing well. We have a product line for that area that's a smaller diameter gun with a larger shaped charge, equal hole design so that it can go through the various tubulars in order to re-frack an existing well. We call that product line our DS Echo if you will. And that's -- we haven't put it together in terms of a piece of literature because it's just part of our standard completion program and perforating programs. But we think that we'll probably do more of that going forward, more marketing on that, because it's with less drilling in some basins, re-fracking is increasing in certain basins.

question: When you talk about private label, you've got some new items. But like global sourcing, I know there's a lot of...
answer: Okay. Yes, sure. Yes, so global sourcing, actually the same exact scenario, right? So as we continue to move, find factories, open new offices, move domestic goods or goods that we're purchasing from an agent to a factory, that all takes time. And you're right. So you get -- usually like for us in FY '13, a lot of that was also back half-loaded that we started seeing benefit from and we'll see that throughout FY '14. And we continue to move that. We continue to see that into FY '14. So yes, they all have lags.

question: I was wondering -- I was very intrigued, Howard, when you talked about trip consolidation. And I was wondering what is it you're seeing, how do you know that there's trip consolidation going on.
answer: Simply the metric of fewer trips and a larger basket size, along with what we're seeing -- is what we're seeing. And that seems to be driving it. Meredith, we get a lot of that information from Nielsen. And so, while we see it certainly in our own register data, we also get the market perspective from Nielsen and IRI.

question: Got you. And then did you guys mention, or I may have missed it, the expected blended interest costs for the financing?
answer: No. It's a little bit early to be talking about interest costs. I will say that, right now, our thought process on the financing is that we would get a secured term loan probably 7 years, senior notes probably at 8 years and then a 5-year ABL in place. Heavy emphasis on that term loan in terms of where the financing comes from, but the ABL would be relatively large also.

question: Understood. And then in terms of the M&A. How's the pipeline looking?
answer: The pipeline is actually wonderful, as we mentioned before, and I'll mention it again. Right now, as you heard us say, we have near-term targets that are valued at anywhere between $60 million to $150 million in revenue. We're actively engaged in various stages with about 21 of them. We have further discussions along the acquisition path of about 4 or 5 of them. And we also have 3 larger revenue opportunities, some larger one might consider to be a transformational type of an acquisition. So our pipeline is robust. We're fully engaged. We have a lot of momentum. We would be the buyer of choice in many of these. And quite candidly, we would say, they're ours to lose. So we're very, very optimistic about the forward activity with our pipeline, as we have been. Again, we've made 6 acquisitions in the past 16 months. So we do have momentum there.

question: Okay, great. And then quickly, this is my last one, would be just the tax rate. It bumped up. It’s little around 40% again this quarter. Just wanted to figure out why it fluctuates on a quarterly basis and where we should try to model that going forward or how do you guys think about it?
answer: The long-term tax rate I would say is 39%. There were some issues that happened this quarter that target to be about 40%, but really the 39% comes from our federal tax rate of 35%. We pay state taxes, which is roughly 3% and then there’s permanent differences. There are certain things we can deduct for tax purposes like meals and entertainment. That adds another 1% and there’s other moving pieces, but I think 39% is a good run rate going forward.

question: Okay. And then to take that one level deeper. The headwinds, obviously, you had mortgage headwinds, payday lending headwinds seemed pretty, I mean, not huge, but certainly material through 2013, and then some FX. Anything else that we should be aware of that crimped the organic growth rate through '13, or stuff that was maybe onetime-ish in nature that won't recur in '14 as we try and think about modeling those business segments -- or business units?
answer: No. I mean, and I'd say it really comes down to the mortgage volumes. And then I think we made progress on all fronts. Payday lending is really small. And it's really de minimus. It's really the mortgage volumes. And I'd say, frankly, I think what -- I think, not only CoreLogic but across the industry, it was a cliff kind of in the late summer, where things kind of dropped pretty sharply versus a gradual tail. That would have been more traditional. So I think that was just -- responding to that sharp drop was a little unusual. But I think we did a great job of cutting costs where we could in the short term, and then putting the '14 plan together. I think the big thing, which I think ultimately is the right thing to happen and will be good for CoreLogic is the -- as the market troughs in '14, which is really -- it's been fueled by a lot of refi volume, obviously, at low interest rates. So as that comes out, purchase market is going to come back because you do have household formation and other more fundamental drivers. So I think that's a good thing for the industry and for CoreLogic, really.

question: So I wanted to ask a little bit about the Q2 EBITDA guidance. I just wanted to double check what the -- if there are any -- or get a listing of the EBITDA adjustments that are going to be part of that in terms of the charges. I know you guys did a good job breaking that out for the Q1.
answer: Yes, I think the big thing, Bill, is we won't have obviously the transactional closing costs as it relates to MSB and DataQuick, so that was almost $10 million in normal fees, et cetera. So that supports the normal balance you get with the seasonality, and then MSB and DataQuick, as you know, it's going to add over $10 million in terms of EBITDA. So we have that lift as well and then we have the continued cost reduction. So those are really the 4 big drivers.

question: Okay. And then the cash flow impact, could you give us an update on what you would anticipate for 2016? The reduced cash payments for losses, what does that mean for your free cash flow?

If you're looking at kind of a year-to-date basis, our paid claims were flat in Title mainly because we paid 2 of the largest claims we've ever paid in our history. It happened in the first half of the year, and that -- those 2 totaled $35 million. So when you back that out, our year-over-year paid claims on a year-to-date basis have fallen significantly. So we feel like they're going to continue to fall as we go into next year. As we talked about at our Investor Day early this year, we feel like there's about a $50 million cash flow pickup on an annualized basis just because of the fact that our paid claims, they're going to continue to fall until they get to that normalized rate.

question: And can you provide any color on how each of the acquired businesses performed during past periods of mortgage market volatility? And I completely understand your point about it being a possibly transformative opportunity.
answer: Yes, I would say that, that -- I think that was discussed earlier, so obviously, LandSafe and RELS are essentially 1 client operations. So they would mirror the outcomes of Bank of America and Wells Fargo. Obviously, Wells Fargo had tremendous success in the mortgage area for many, many years. question: Just for my follow-up, the guidance raise I know was predicated on roughly flat number of loans year-over-year versus a prior expectation, I think, for a decline of around 15% or, I guess, it's an improvement now over around a couple of hundred billion dollars from a prior expectation in volume. question: Just a question. answer: Yes. Look, there is a tremendous amount of money going into housing and mortgage. And I think, by the way, that's being put in by new players and existing players. So some of these players are -- we're partnering with and they are using our data. So it's -- I see it as all kind of all good, if you will, in terms of our potential growth as we go forward. A lot going into being a 2% or 3% brokerage. I don't know about how those models will end up. But I think in terms of adding value to the mortgage constituencies, I think we'll do that. And I think the -- anything that makes the housing experience better is good for CoreLogic, and we'll be there to contribute because the property data is necessary no matter who it is and no matter what they're doing.

question: That's great to hear. Look, can I just ask one follow-up, on the property intelligence risk management side, the -- look, I mean, at the end of the day, the growth rate there is still relatively flattish. And I guess I'm curious, especially if you back out Symbility. I mean, it looks like organic growth, correct me if I'm wrong, was down a little bit, maybe 1% or 2%? I'm just curious what you see as the drivers to get that more -- to reaccelerate that?
answer: Yes. Look, I think the organic -- so I think a couple of things, Darrin. One is, I think I would characterize the growth rate as kind of flat last year for a number of reasons. But I think we did have the Australian market compressed for the first time in like 3 decades. So we have -- those guys were down in the upper teens in terms of market volumes. Currency, it's amazing how low some of these currencies are in the U.S. dollar. So that we took a haircut there. I think the fundamental product offerings and the client relationships are very strong. I feel pretty good about the -- some very significant product offerings that are going to hit the market. question: Okay. Great. So are you seeing a positive mix benefit here where more of the purchase is also coming from just higher priced markets that's driving your fee up kind of in line with home price appreciation?
answer:
Yes, we are. And just -- I mean, overall, the market is very strong right now. And on this topic, by the way, we're very optimistic, right, the real demographics are positive for us. We had a very strong spring selling season. I'll say in July right now, we're starting to trend a little more towards, I call it, the seasonal market. We're probably down about 6% on all accounts right now in July. 
And also, we think that the purchase market also is starting to stabilize a little more normalized, if you will. The inventories are ticking up a little bit. We're seeing less crazy bidding rules. We probably see less property appreciation in the year and for the next year or so. And all of those trends to us is a positive sign, not a negative. It makes the market more sustainable than normal. So we think it's going to be a really good second half of the year. We think '22 is going to be a good year for purchase too.

question: Okay. Great. Last question for me just on share repurchases. It looks like you picked up the volume pretty significantly in January. Just how are you balancing share repurchases with other investment opportunities and how -- maybe how we should be forecasting repurchases in '22 and '23?
answer:
Well, it's always something we look at. I mean we're -- we've been very active in the M&A market, certainly last year and more. We're very active in terms of investing in our core of business just to develop software and tools to make it easier for us to digitally connect with our customers. So we're making a lot of investments. And we're fortunate in the fact that we can make those investments and still repurchase our shares. We think that our stock is undervalued, and that's why we're buying our shares. I mean when you look at our multiple on my Bloomberg this morning, we were trading at 11x earnings. But we kind of ask ourselves where are we in the cycle? At 11x earnings that would kind of imply we're at the peak of the cycle, but we're certainly not peak when it comes to refis or at the trough when it comes to refis. We're certainly not peak when it comes to investment income, or at the trough when it comes to investment income. 
So you balance out those and I think on a stand-alone basis, our multiples maybe should be a little bit higher. But then when you layer in some assets that we have at First American that maybe aren't completely reflected in our public market value, including Ken mentioned our proptech portfolio, the carrying value of the portfolio was $673 million at the end of the year. And when you trade on a PE basis, at least I would argue that that's not being fully reflected in the value of our shares. 
And then certainly, we have some assets that we have losses in First American. We're very excited about Endpoint. Endpoint has losses. Same thing for ServiceMac, same thing for our property and casualty business. But we feel like all those have value to them that aren't being reflected. 
And so for those reasons, we -- we've been in the market these last couple of months, and we'll kind of see what happens for the rest of the year. I don't have like a forecast for you. But as we mentioned in earlier calls, we're going to be more likely to buy back in the future than we have in the past. And I think we've started to show that.
